name: Organizations diverging from their founders' intentions
plain_explanation: Russell's general observation that institutions, once established, often take on a life of their own quite different from what their founders originally intended.
precise_definition: Russell's claim, illustrated by the Benedictine Order and (he says) most strikingly by the Catholic Church as a whole, that 'organizations have a life of their own, independent of the intentions of their founders' -- so that vows of poverty and obedience can, in practice, produce great wealth and near-sovereign power for those who take them.
why_it_mattered: It frames Russell's account of how an ascetic, otherworldly movement became, over time, wealthy, learned, and politically powerful -- outcomes Russell treats as not uniformly regrettable, since they include the Order's later contributions to scholarship.
historical_origin: Illustrated with Gibbon's quoted anecdote of a Benedictine abbot: 'My vow of poverty has given me an hundred thousand crowns a year; my vow of obedience has raised me to the rank of a sovereign prince.'
examples: The wealth and secular power later Benedictine abbots accumulated despite vows of poverty and obedience
The Catholic Church's own historical transformation, which Russell says 'would astonish Jesus, and even Paul'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: A general observation Russell applies directly to religious institutions in this chapter.
